56. The Halo Effect

The Halo Effect is a cognitive bias where positive impressions in one area shape the overall perception of a person, company, brand, or product for an individual. This phenomenon leads evaluators to be swayed by prior judgments of performance or personality, often clouding their ability to form an objective view based on all available evidence.

The term was coined by psychologist Edward Thorndike in 1920, following experiments in which commanding officers rated subordinates on traits such as intelligence, physique, leadership and character without direct interaction. Taller, more attractive service members were consistently rated as more intelligent and capable, revealing how a single favourable trait can skew perceptions of the entire character of a person. Thorndike, a controversial figure due to his support for eugenics, noted that people tend to generalise from one standout quality to form an overly favourable impression.

"I hope to have made it clear that we have much to learn about eugenics, and also that we already know enough to justify us in providing for the original intellect and character of man in the future with a higher, purer source than the muddy streams of the past. If it is our duty to improve the face of the world and human customs and traditions, so that men unborn may live in better conditions, it is doubly our duty to improve the original natures of these men themselves. For there is no surer means of improving the conditions of life."

The Halo Effect can manifest in everyday scenarios, such as when an individual perceives someone in a well-groomed, attractive photograph as inherently good or competent, based on a mental heuristic rooted in personal biases, preferences, or social norms. This snap judgment often reflects the ideologies, aspirations, or prejudices of an individual, rather than objective reality. For instance, in online dating, an appealing appearance might lead others to assume the person is kind, intelligent, or trustworthy, despite no evidence linking physical attractiveness to these traits. Conversely, the “devil effect” occurs when a single negative trait taints the overall perception of a person or entity.

This bias has far-reaching implications across various domains, including hiring decisions, performance evaluations, consumer behaviour and personal relationships. When a single positive attribute overshadows other qualities, it can obscure a balanced assessment of strengths and weaknesses, leading to flawed judgments and suboptimal decisions. In professional settings, a charismatic employee might be rated higher than their performance warrants, while in consumerism, a celebrity endorsement might inflate the perceived value of a product.

The Halo Effect also fuels stereotyping and overgeneralisation. By assuming one positive trait applies universally, individuals may make sweeping judgments about a person or group, overlooking individual differences and perpetuating stereotypes. This can hinder a nuanced understanding of others and reinforce biased assumptions.

The influence of the Halo Effect extends to diverse contexts: in management, a likable employee might be favoured despite average performance; in jury decisions, an eloquent defendant might seem more trustworthy; in celebrity endorsements, a famous face can elevate the appeal of a product; in classrooms, a well-mannered student might be perceived as more capable; and even in choosing fruit, an unblemished apple might be deemed superior despite being laden with dangerous pesticides. Awareness of this bias is critical to fostering fairer evaluations and better decision-making across these scenarios.
